Course Description

To provide students with practical Microsoft Word 2021 and 365 skills for producing professional business documents. Students will learn features common across Microsoft Office applications, build tables and an effective resume, format multi-page reports with headers, footers, citations, and a bibliography, design a promotional brochure using graphics and page layout tools, and use Mail Merge to generate personalized letters, envelopes, and labels.

items.title: Introduction to Microsoft Office — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Overview Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 2-4 · Overview Chapter 1 · CBO Objectives: Describe similarities and differences between Office 2021, Microsoft 365, and Office Online / Identify uses of cloud storage

What Devices Will Microsoft Office Work With?

Office works on desktops, laptops/notebooks, all-in-one PCs and Macs, and Windows, Android, and iOS phones and tablets (Publisher and Access are Windows-PC-only). The book assumes you're working on a desktop, laptop, or all-in-one computer. For more on operating system and device compatibility, do a web search for “Microsoft Office 2021 products.”

What Storage Does Microsoft Office Provide?

OneDrive is the cloud storage bundled with Office 2021 and Microsoft 365 — it lets you access your files from any device with an internet or Wi-Fi connection. Storage ranges from 5GB to 5TB depending on the product, and OneDrive can be used as your primary storage or as a backup; it's faster than emailing files to yourself. For more, do a web search for “OneDrive.”

Which Microsoft Office Should I Use?

Microsoft Office comes in three distinct formats:

  • Office Online — free, requires a Microsoft account, no installation, browser-based, with limited features; good for simple tasks, but requires internet access.
  • Microsoft Office 2021 — purchased once and installed on one PC; no internet required to run it; does not include all Microsoft 365 features, and you must pay for future major upgrades. Plans may include Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote, Outlook, Publisher, Access, Skype, and Teams.
  • Microsoft 365 (formerly Office 365) — a monthly or annual subscription for one or more devices (PC, Mac, or mobile); all upgrades are included, so you always have the “latest-and-greatest” version; may include features not available in Office 2021.

This book's own examples assume Office 2021 desktop or a Microsoft 365 subscription running on Windows 10/11 — if you're using Microsoft 365, your screen may not match every illustration exactly, since Microsoft 365 can change after a book's publication.

What Are the Microsoft Office Apps?

{{img:3.png|Textbook page 3 — the Microsoft Office app icon tables}}

The four core Office apps:

  • Word — word processing: letters, reports, essays, business plans
  • Excel — spreadsheets: rows and columns, calculations, budgets, loan interest
  • Access — database: tables, forms, reports, queries
  • PowerPoint — presentations: tell a story, market a product, explain a concept

Additional Office apps:

  • OneNote — note-taking: handwritten or typed notes, audio, screen captures
  • Outlook — email, tasks, calendars, meetings, contacts, notes
  • Publisher — desktop publishing: newsletters, brochures
  • Skype — audio, video, text, file, and screen sharing
  • Teams — workplace video calling, chat, and sharing across groups

Microsoft Accounts

A Microsoft account gives you access to your settings, files, contacts, and more; it can include Hotmail, Bing, MSN, Office, OneDrive, Outlook.com, Skype, Store, Windows, or Xbox Live credentials. Once you're logged in on a device, you're logged in across every Office app. To create one for free, do a web search for “Microsoft account.”

items.title: The Ribbon, the Quick Access Toolbar & Undo/Redo — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Overview Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 4 · Overview Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Identify parts of the Office user interface

The Ribbon

The Ribbon displays along the top of every Office app window, with tabs and buttons/icons specific to that app. Buttons are arranged in groups within each tab, and some tabs, groups, and commands are common across the whole suite. This book focuses on the Word Ribbon, and specifically the Home, Insert, Design, Layout, References, Mailings, Review, and View tabs.

The Quick Access Toolbar

The Quick Access Toolbar (QAT) is a one-line toolbar in the top-left corner, present by default in every app. It holds frequently-used commands and is customizable per app — the Word, Excel, Access, PowerPoint, and Outlook QATs are all independent of one another.

Undo/Redo

Undo reverses a typed action or command, as long as the app hasn't been closed since. Redo reapplies an action you just undid. The text on the Undo/Redo buttons changes based on the last action you performed.

Note: Some actions — like saving or sharing a file — cannot be undone.

Path: Quick Access toolbar → Undo or Redo

items.title: Backstage View, Program Options & Saving Files — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Overview Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 6-7 · Overview Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Identify Office features available through Backstage view

Backstage View

The File tab's Backstage view is your “personal manager” for the open file and app — from here you can update file info and account settings, open, save, print, share, and export files, give feedback, and recover unsaved files. These are big-picture, file-level actions, distinct from the task-level commands you'll find on the other Ribbon tabs.

Program Options

File → Options lets you set your preferences for each app — your username and initials, whether formatting marks are displayed, spelling correction behavior, and your default save location. The Word Options → Save pane, for example, includes an AutoSave OneDrive/SharePoint toggle, a file format dropdown, and an AutoRecover interval (5 minutes by default) with a “keep the last AutoRecovered version” checkbox.

Path: File → Options

Saving Files

Save is used the first time you save a file — it triggers the Save As screen so you can choose a name and location. After that, using Save again just updates the file in place.

Note: The AutoSave toggle sits to the left of the Quick Access Toolbar.

A good rule of thumb: save your file as often as you can afford to lose data — for example, every minute.

Path: File → Save or Save As

Finding, Searching, and Opening Files

You can open a file through the Open dialog, a list of recently-saved files within the app, File Explorer, or the Windows Search box.

Sharing Files via Email and with People

You can share a file directly from the app to email or to OneDrive; sharing via OneDrive sends a link to the file.

Tip: The Share button is in the top-right corner of the app window.

Path: File → Share → Email  |  File → Share → Share with People

The book's own Develop Your Skills O1-D3 exercise for this topic is an interactive WebSim, not a Word document — it's available through the ebook or Labyrinth's Student Resource Center if you'd like extra practice sharing a file with people, but it isn't a graded assignment in this course.

Printing

Before you print, run Spelling & Grammar, proofread your document, verify your formats, and check your page count. Use Print Preview, and remember you can print to paper or to PDF (an eco-friendly option).

Path: File → Print

A template is a document, worksheet, or presentation with fonts, paragraph styles, and page layout already built in. Installed sample templates ship with the app, or you can search online templates from File → New's Search box, arranged by category (business, personal, industry).

Path: File → New

items.title: Common Features on the Home Tab & the Office Clipboard — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Overview Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 9-11 · Overview Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Use the Office Clipboard

Common Features on the Home Tab

On the Home tab, you'll use Microsoft Word to Cut, Copy, and Paste with the Office Clipboard, format text, use the Mini toolbar, and find and replace text.

The Office Clipboard

The Clipboard is located at the far left of the Home tab. Its dialog-box launcher opens the Clipboard pane, which shows thumbnails of your most recent cuts and copies (most recent at top) — you can paste any item repeatedly, or clear them all. Think of Cut like a scrapbook: it removes the original and pastes it at the target. Copy leaves the original in place and pastes a duplicate.

The Clipboard Features table below summarizes each Clipboard command:

FeatureWhat It Does
CutRemoves the original selection from the source location and places it on the Clipboard.
CopyCreates a duplicate of the original selection (stays in source) and places a copy on the Clipboard.
PasteInserts the most recent Clipboard item at the target; three paste-option buttons: Keep Source Formatting (retains source formats), Merge Formatting (combines source and target formats), Keep Text Only (takes on target's formatting only).
Format PainterApplies character and paragraph formatting from a source selection to other text; double-click for multi-use, Esc or click again to turn off.

Path: Home → Clipboard → Cut (Ctrl+X)  |  Home → Clipboard → Copy (Ctrl+C)  |  Home → Clipboard → Paste (Ctrl+V)

Formatting Text Using Font Group Settings

Select your text first, then use the Font group's buttons, or open the Font dialog box launcher for the full range of formatting options.

Format Painter copies formatting the way a paint can applies paint — select the source formatting, click Format Painter once to apply it a single time, or double-click it to apply it multiple times in a row; press Esc (or click Format Painter again) to turn it off.

items.title: Other Common Features: Help, Search & Taking Screenshots — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Overview Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 18-19 · Overview Chapter 1 · CBO Objectives: Search for Help within Office applications / Capture a screen in an Office application

Help and Search

The Search box at the top of the app window gives you quick access to commands, features, definitions, or links to Help documentation. You can also right-click a selected word or phrase and choose Search to open the Search pane (this needs an internet connection). Press F1 to open a list of Help topics.

Tell Me More

The Tell Me More link appears at the bottom of some button tooltips — clicking it opens the Help window with more detail on that feature, without you having to type any search text.

{{img:18.png|Textbook page 18 — the Tell Me More link on the Text Effects and Typography tooltip}}

Taking Screenshots

The Screenshot button captures the entire window, or part of a window, from any other open application. The Screenshot dropdown's Available Windows gallery shows thumbnails of every open app window, updating live as apps open and close — click a thumbnail to insert a full-window screenshot. Screen Clipping lets you drag-select just a portion of a window instead.

Day 2 · Chapter 1: Creating and Editing Business Documents

Day 2 Overview

Build a well-formatted business letter while learning to navigate, enter, select, and edit text, create numbered and bulleted lists, use document views, and save documents as different file types.

Competencies Covered Today

  • Navigate in a document
  • Enter, select, and edit text

Project: Creating a Well-Formatted Business Letter

Opening narrative (Chapter 1, p. 21):

“In the employment world, few skills are more valued than effective formal writing. Business-to-business communication is an essential element of the employment network; it’s the oil that keeps the whole machine running. You can help further your company’s goals by crafting effective business letters that are formal, succinct, and engaging. Of course, in our digital age, simply writing a letter is only half the picture; skills in digital word processing are just as critical. In this chapter, you will create and format a well-crafted business letter that is perfect for the digital age.”

Project: Creating a Well-Formatted Business Letter

“School is over, and it’s time to line up some interviews. You are seeking a position in the technology field. You’ve scanned lots of ads and websites, and found a few job openings you’re interested in. You know the hiring process will be competitive for most of these positions. To give yourself an edge, you’ll need to draft a stellar cover letter—one that will get you noticed right from the start.”

This is the running narrative for the whole day: playing the role of job-seeker Stella Martin, you’ll build and progressively edit a cover letter addressed to Mr. Blake Carter, Hiring Manager at Global Computer Sales and Service, applying for a Retail Computer Sales Representative position — across every Hands-On exercise today, W1-D2 through W1-D7.

items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 22-23 · Chapter 1 · background knowledge — sets up today’s business-letter project

Elements of a Professional Business Letter

There are several acceptable business letter styles; all contain similar elements but with varied formatting. This chapter uses block style (the most common) — all elements left-aligned. Every business letter contains these elements:

  • Date — two inches from top of page (may vary based on letterhead)
  • Inside address — two to four lines below the date
  • Salutation — followed by a colon (e.g., “Dear Mr. Carter:”)
  • Body
  • Complimentary close — followed by a comma (e.g., “Sincerely,”)
  • Signature
{{img:22.png|Textbook page 22 — a labeled example business letter from Global Computer Sales and Service, addressed to Mr. Blake Carter and signed by Stella Martin}}

Note: The spacing shown in some parts of the example letters in this chapter is not standard, and the business letter you will be creating also does not use standard spacing. That’s because these are the spacing settings in the default blank Word template. Line and paragraph spacing will be adjusted in another chapter.

What’s Important in a Cover Letter?

  • Purpose: Use a cover letter to introduce yourself and explain why you fit the job requirements.
  • Application Tracking System (ATS): First review of application documents is often done by an ATS program; research how to write documents so they aren’t overlooked.
  • File Types: Some file types work better than others for ATS; some employers request a specific file type.
  • Audience Awareness: Study the job description and research the company online.
  • Beginning, Middle, and End: Introduce yourself with an attention grabber; highlight (don’t duplicate) résumé points; close expressing enthusiasm.
  • Importance of Fresh Eyes: Ask friends/colleagues to proof your documents.

Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 23-24 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Navigate in a document

Navigating with the Scroll Bar

The scroll bar lets you navigate through a document but does not move the insertion point — after scrolling, you must click in the document to reposition it. There are two ways to use it: click the up/down arrows to scroll one line at a time, or drag the scroll box to move quickly through a multipage document. Clicking in the gray area above or below the scroll box moves one screen at a time. When the mouse pointer is positioned inside the text area, it resembles an uppercase “I” (an I-beam); the insertion point begins flashing wherever you click.

Keyboard Navigation Tips

  • Right/left arrow keys move the insertion point one character right/left; up/down arrow keys move one line up/down.
  • [Ctrl]+[End] moves to the end of the document.
  • [Ctrl]+[Home] moves to the beginning of the document.
  • [End] moves to the end of the line.
  • [Home] moves to the beginning of the line.

Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book page: 25 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Enter, select, and edit text

Entering Text

Text appears at the flashing insertion point; inserting text pushes existing text to the right. Word Wrap automatically moves text to the next line at the right-hand margin, so there’s no need to press Enter at the end of each line.

Using the Enter Key

Enter begins a new paragraph or inserts blank lines. Anything ending with Enter counts as a paragraph — so short lines like a date line, an inside address line, or even a blank line are each their own “paragraph.” Enter inserts a paragraph symbol (¶), visible only when formatting marks are shown.

Showing and Hiding Formatting Marks

Formatting marks appear on screen but never print. They’re useful for determining whether the space between words was made with the Spacebar or Tab. Toggle formatting marks on and off with Home → Paragraph → Show/Hide ¶.

Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 26-28 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Enter, select, and edit text

Selecting Text

You must select (highlight) text before performing an action on it. The most common method is to click-and-drag the I-beam, but there are more efficient methods:

  • Double-click to select a single word.
  • Triple-click to select a paragraph.
  • [Ctrl]+click anywhere within a sentence to select that single sentence (first letter through the period).
  • Hover in the left margin and click to the left of a line to select that single line.
  • Click and drag to quickly select multiple lines.

Note: The Mini toolbar appears when text is selected; ignore it and it fades away.

Additional Mouse and Keyboard Combinations

  • Click, hold Shift, click elsewhere to select awkward or large blocks of text.
  • [Ctrl]+click to select a sentence.
  • [Ctrl]+[A] to select the entire document.

Tip: On a Mac, use the Cmd key in place of Ctrl for the same shortcuts.

Select Nonadjacent Text

You can select multiple, non-contiguous locations at the same time — double-click one word, then hold [Ctrl] and double-click another word; both selections remain active. You can select as many nonadjacent areas as you’d like using [Ctrl].

items.body:
Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 28-30 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Create numbered and bulleted lists

Using Numbered and Bulleted Lists

Numbered and bulleted lists draw attention to items of interest; they can be turned on before typing or applied afterward. Numbered lists automatically renumber when items are inserted or deleted. Use a numbered list when sequence matters; use a bulleted list when it does not. Once a list item is created, pressing Enter creates a new item; Tab demotes an item (indents it right, creating a sublevel), and Shift+Tab promotes it (moves it back left). Items can be demoted up to eight sublevels deep.

Note: Check whether a prospective employer’s ATS can read numbered/bulleted lists.

Ribbon paths: Home → Paragraph → Bullets and Home → Paragraph → Numbering.

Continue a Numbered List

Choosing Numbering again after a break restarts numbering at 1 by default. A smart tag (AutoCorrect Options) appears, offering Continue Numbering to resume the prior list’s sequence instead. Right-clicking the number also offers Restart at 1 from the context menu.

Hands-On W1-D4: Create Numbered and Bulleted Lists

Hands-On Exercise

Part 1 — Practice with a Numbered List

  1. Choose File → Save As and save your letter as W1-D4-CoverLtr.
  2. Show formatting marks if they aren’t already visible.
  3. Position the insertion point at the end of the last line of the first body paragraph, tap Enter twice, and type: “My college education provided me with the following technical skills that will allow me to make a positive contribution to Global Computer:” then tap Enter.

(Try intentionally misspelling “experience” on item 4 and watch AutoCorrect fix it as you tap Spacebar.)
  5. Tap Enter three times at the end of item 4 — this generates the next number, then turns numbering off and adds paragraph spacing.

Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 30-31 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Enter, select, and edit text

Editing Text

Backspace and Delete remove one character at a time; select a block of text first to remove or replace it in one action. The spell checker underlines potential misspellings with a red squiggly line; the grammar checker underlines potential grammar issues with a double blue line. Both are right-clickable for suggestions, but they are aids only — human judgment is still required.

Synonyms and Thesaurus

Right-click a word and choose Synonyms from the shortcut menu to see a short list of quick alternatives, or choose Thesaurus from that same submenu to open the full Thesaurus task pane.

Hands-On Exercise

  2. In the first line, position the insertion point before “advertised,” type “Representative”, then tap Spacebar (the job title becomes “Retail Computer Sales Representative”).
  3. In the third line, position the insertion point between “a” and “n” in “an,” tap Delete to remove the “n,” tap Spacebar, and type “sales” (turning “an intern” into “a sales intern”).

  5. In the second paragraph, double-click “college” and tap Delete, so “My college education” becomes “My education.”
  6. In the third bullet of the second (sales-skills) list, double-click “articulating” and tap Delete, then type “clearly stating” in its place.
  7. Work with Synonyms: right-click “appropriate” (third bullet, first list), choose Synonyms, and select “suitable.”
  8. Right-click “Adeptness” (second bullet, second list), choose Synonyms, and select “Expertise.”
  9. Save your file.

I am applying for the position of Retail Computer Sales Representative advertised on your website. I am a recent Computer Science graduate from Case Western University, where I attained a 3.9 GPA. During the summers, I worked as a sales intern at Best Computers in Cleveland. I am extremely interested in discussing your sales position, which aligns well with my education and sales experience.

My education provided me with the following technical skills that will allow me to make a positive contribution to Global Computer.

  • An understanding of real-world computer needs
  • An awareness of the latest technologies available
  • The ability to analyze problems and apply the suitable hardware and software solutions
  • Hands-on experience with a wide variety of computer equipment

My experience at Best Computers provided me with the following sales-related knowledge that would benefit Global Computer:

  • Skill in using consultative sales skills to learn about clients’ needs
  • Expertise in analyzing client requirements and addressing their business issues
  • Competence in clearly stating solutions and demonstrating product benefits to the client
  • Proficiency in handling objections
  • Ability to provide a training and implementation plan that ensures high customer satisfaction

I am impressed with your excellent products and reputation. I am confident that I am a strong candidate, and I will contact you in the near future to arrange an interview.

Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 32-34 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Use document views

Working with Views

You can view a document multiple ways. Views change the document’s on-screen appearance but, in most cases, do not affect the printed document’s appearance. Views are chosen from the View tab or from the status bar.

Document Views

ViewDescription
Read ModeBooklike reading experience, pages laid out side by side; Ribbon disappears; navigate horizontally as in a book.
Print LayoutDefault view; documents look as they will when printed — graphics, headers/footers, multi-column layouts visible.
Web LayoutDisplays the document as it would look as a web page — one long page, no page breaks.
OutlineUseful for organizing long documents.
DraftSimplifies page layout by eliminating headers, footers, and graphic elements; useful when focusing on content.

Note: Depending on your screen resolution, both pages of a document may already be visible in Read Mode, in which case the side-arrow navigation control will be inactive.

Day 2 · Chapter 1 Reading

Book pages: 33-34 · Chapter 1 · CBO Objective: Save documents as different file types

Saving Your Work in a Different Format

A file’s format is set by its filename extension. Note: Windows may hide file extensions by default.

Document Files

Earlier versions of Word used the .doc format; the current version uses .docx. Files saved in .doc format may not open correctly in newer readers if saved as .docx; conversely, you can save a document down to .doc format for compatibility with older versions. Opening an older-format file shows (Compatibility Mode) in the title bar, meaning features that aren’t compatible with older versions are turned off.

PDF Files

PDF is great for sharing since the layout and fonts render identically across devices, operating systems, and software. A prospective employer may request application documents be submitted as a PDF.

Saving a Document for ATS Analysis

items.title: What's Important in a Résumé? & Introducing Tables — Reading
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 36-38 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objectives: Create a table; Select data in a table

What’s Important in a Résumé?

The purpose of a résumé is to win an interview; hiring managers take less than a minute to review one, so it must be dynamic, targeted, and emphasize experience, qualifications, and skills that transfer to the job. One page is generally preferred. There are three primary résumé types:

  • Chronological — most recent position listed first, shows career-path growth.
  • Functional — skill- and accomplishment-based; good for new graduates, career changers, or those with employment gaps.
  • Combination — skills/experience listed first, then employment history.

Introducing Tables

Tables organize and align data in an easy-to-read format and break up text-heavy documents. There are multiple ways to insert a table, all found on the Insert tab, Tables group: the Table button, the Insert Table dialog box, and the Quick Tables gallery; tabbed columns can also be converted to a table. Contextual tabs appear on the Ribbon when the insertion point is positioned in a table.

Creating New Tables

Tables are organized in columns and rows; where a column and row intersect is called a cell.

{{img:36.png|Textbook page 36 diagram labeling a table's Row, Column, and Cell}}

You choose the number of rows and columns when you create the table, and you can add or remove either later.

Navigating and Selecting Data in a Table

Keystrokes for moving around a table: Tab moves to the next cell; Shift+Tab moves to the previous cell; the arrow keys move to adjacent cells.

To format or modify table content, you must select it first. The mouse pointer changes shape depending on whether you’re selecting a cell, row, column, or the entire table. The move handle (the small square that appears at the table’s top-left corner) moves or selects the entire table.

  • Hover over the left margin next to a row and use the selection arrow to select that row.
  • Click the move handle to select the entire table.
  • Hover just above the table’s top border and use the down-pointing black arrow to select a column.

Additional navigation notes: Tab and Shift+Tab move one cell at a time; tapping Tab at the end of a row that isn’t the last row moves to the start of the next row; Alt+Page Up moves to the top of a column; Alt+Page Down moves to the end of a column.

Note: The Mini toolbar appears when you select table data, just as when you select regular text.

items.title: Modifying a Table: Inserting Rows and Columns, Merging/Splitting Cells, Aligning Data — Reading
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 38-40 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objectives: Format tables; Select data in a table

Modifying a Table

The contextual (Table) Layout tab holds all table-structure-modification features; some are also available via a right-click pop-up menu.

Note: Contextual tabs can share a name with a regular Ribbon tab — this book will specify “(Table) Layout” whenever referring to the contextual version.

Inserting Rows and Columns

Insert multiple rows or columns by first selecting that many existing rows or columns. You can add a row to the bottom of a table by tapping Tab while in the last cell. For a quick single row or column insert, hover just above or to the left of the table between two rows or columns until the insert control (a + icon) appears, then click it. Path: (Table) Layout → Rows & Columns, or right-click → Insert.

Merging/Splitting Cells and Aligning Data

You can merge two or more adjacent cells in a row or column into a single cell — commonly used to create a heading row that spans the full width of the table — or split a single cell into multiple cells. You can also split an entire table into two: position the insertion point in the row that should start the second table and run Split Table. A paragraph mark appears between the two resulting tables; deleting that paragraph mark rejoins them. Path: (Table) Layout → Merge → Merge Cells / Split Cells, or right-click; Split Table is also under (Table) Layout → Merge.

Aligning Table Data: you can align data horizontally and vertically within a cell, change text direction, and modify cell margins. Path: (Table) Layout → Alignment.

Book pages: 44-46 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objectives: Format tables; Apply table styles

Formatting with Borders, Shading, and Styles

The contextual Table Design tab holds borders, shading, and styles tools; the (Table) Layout tab can convert an entire table (or selected parts of it) to plain text. The Borders and Shading buttons have “memory” — they reflect the last option chosen, which is handy for repeat application. Borders can be removed while gridlines remain on-screen as a build guide — gridlines never print. Table text can also be formatted using Home tab tools or the Mini toolbar. When selecting a table style, hover over it first for Live Preview before committing.

{{img:45.png|Textbook page 45 demonstrating the Table Design tab's Shading button being used to apply Gray, Accent 3, Darker 25% shading to a selected table row}}

Specific mechanics shown above: Table Design → Borders → Borders menu ↓ → No Border removes all borders; selecting the first row and choosing Outside Borders adds a border around just that row; with the row still selected, Table Design → Table Styles → Shading menu ↓ applies a shading color (e.g., “Gray, Accent 3, Darker 25%”).

Table Styles gallery: Table Design → Table Styles → the More button opens the full gallery (e.g., the “Grid Table 5 Dark – Accent 1” style used in today’s exercise).

Note: The style overrides your cell margin spacing, borders, and shading. In turn, you can override Table Styles formatting by applying direct formatting.

Convert Table to Text

(Table) Layout → Data → Convert to Text opens a dialog offering separator options (Paragraph Marks is used in today’s exercise) — this can be used to detach a header/contact-info row from a table without changing how it looks.

items.title: Working with Print and Print Preview & What to Do Before a Job Interview — Reading
items.body:
Day 3 · Chapter 2 Reading

Book pages: 47-48 · Chapter 2 · CBO Objective: Print documents

Working with Print and Print Preview

The Print command and Print Preview live in Backstage view: File → Print, or [Ctrl]+[P]. The Settings area controls the number of copies and printer selection; the printer menu includes a “print to PDF” option (e.g., Microsoft Print to PDF or Microsoft XPS Document Writer). The right side of the Print screen previews how the document will look when printed.

Note: If you printed to PDF, remember to switch back to your default printer next time.

What to Do Before a Job Interview

This is real-world career-readiness content, not a Word-skills topic. Job search sites (Indeed.com, LinkedIn.com) offer interviewing tips, and a web search for “interview tips” can help.

  • Anticipate the questions the interviewer might ask and prepare answers — you can search “interview questions for [specific career]”.
  • Practice by role-playing with a friend or colleague.
  • Prepare your own questions to ask the interviewer.
  • Research appropriate dress — search “how to dress for an interview”; when in doubt, dress conservatively; it’s OK to ask the person scheduling the interview about the company’s dress code.
  • What to bring: driving directions/contact info, a folder or briefcase, paper copies of your résumé, a pen, and a notepad.
  • What NOT to bring: earbuds, a phone that isn’t turned off, a baseball cap, chewing gum, food or drink, or distracting jewelry.

items.title: Creating a Business Report — Setting Margins & Indenting Text — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 50 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Work with columns and set margins

Creating a Business Report

Reports are important documents often used in business and education to distribute information, communicate ideas, and share viewpoints and plans on a variety of topics. Before writing a business report: plan before you write, know your audience, use active voice, avoid wordiness, use plain language (avoid overblown words), don’t use clichés, use parallel structure, edit out anything that doesn’t add meaning, and organize your writing into short sections.

Setting Margins

Margins are the white space around the edges of a page; they can be set for an entire document, a section, or selected text. The default margin in the Blank Document and Single Spaced (Blank) templates is 1” all around. A gallery of margin presets is available, or you can specify custom margins.

Ribbon path: Layout → Page Setup → Margins.

Indenting Text

Indents offset text from the margins. You can set an indent using the Ribbon’s Increase Indent / Decrease Indent buttons (these affect the left indent only, in the default half-inch tab-stop increments), or by dragging the indent markers on the ruler.

{{img:50.png|Textbook page 50 diagram of the ruler's four indent markers (First Line Indent, Hanging Indent, Left Indent, Right Indent), with a side-by-side comparison of a Standard Indent and a Hanging Indent shown on the ruler and in paragraph text}}

Ribbon path: Home → Paragraph → Increase Indent / Decrease Indent.

Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 52-53 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Format text and apply styles

Setting Custom Tab Stops

Default tab stops are set every half inch.

Warning: “Never use the Spacebar key to line up columns. Even if it looks right on the screen, it most likely will not print correctly.”

Using the Ruler to Set Custom Tabs

There are four tab types — left, right, center, and decimal — all settable via the ruler. The insertion point must be in the target line before you set a tab. Tab settings are stored in the paragraph symbol, so they carry to the next line when you tap [Enter].

Tip: Drag a tab off the ruler to delete it.

Using the Tabs Dialog Box to Set Custom Tabs

The Tabs dialog box is an alternative to the ruler — it lets you specify precise tab positions, tab type/alignment, clear tabs, and set dot-leader tabs (common in a table of contents).

Ribbon path: Home → Paragraph dialog box launcher → Tabs…

Formatting Text and Using Styles

A style is “a group of formats” that lets you apply multiple formats at once, based on the template’s theme (colors, fonts, graphic effects). Styles standardize headings, titles, and special character formats.

Spacing in Letters

Word 2021’s default line spacing is 1.08 (not 1.0), which adds about 8% extra space between lines plus 8 points after each paragraph — so you only tap Enter once at the end of a paragraph. Business documents (letters, reports, proposals) typically need traditional single spacing. There are two methods to get it: (1) use the Single Spaced (Blank) template from File → New, or (2) use the Line and Paragraph Spacing button (Home → Paragraph).

Ribbon path: Home → Paragraph → Line and Paragraph Spacing, or Right-click → Paragraph → Line Spacing.

items.title: Types of Styles & Collapsing Heading Topics — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 58-59 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Format text and apply styles

Types of Styles

Word has two basic types of styles, and understanding the difference matters for how much of your document a style affects:

  • Character styles — apply to selected characters only, not the whole paragraph. Font and bold formatting are examples. You must select the exact text you want affected before applying a character style.
  • Paragraph styles — apply to the paragraph containing the insertion point (or to selected paragraphs), affecting things like line spacing. A paragraph style can also include character formats — for example, a heading style might combine a bold font with paragraph spacing. Unlike a character style, you don’t need to select the whole paragraph first; simply placing the insertion point inside it is enough.

Ribbon path: Home → Styles → Styles Gallery, or Home → Styles dialog box launcher.

Collapsing Heading Topics

Applying a heading style with the insertion point in the heading reveals a small triangle marker at the left of the heading; clicking it collapses or expands the text below it. This is illustrated in the book with “The Net Generation” heading shown both collapsed and expanded.

items.title: Arranging Text in Multiple Columns — Column Breaks and Section Breaks — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 62-64 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Work with columns and set margins

Arranging Text in Multiple Columns

Newspaper-style (newsletter-style) columns let text flow down one column and wrap to the top of the next, enhancing readability by breaking up dense text with gaps; columns reflow automatically as text is edited. Set columns via the Columns button or the Columns dialog box (presets: One/Two/Three/Left/Right; you can also set custom widths/spacing and a line-between option).

Ribbon path: Layout → Page Setup → Columns, or → More Columns.

Column Breaks and Section Breaks

A column break manually forces a column to end — for example, to put a heading at the top of the next column, or to balance columns on the last page. A section break is required whenever a document-level formatting change (like switching from a 1-column to a 2-column layout) doesn’t apply to the whole document.

Section BreakPurpose
Next PageStarts new section on next page
ContinuousStarts new section on same page
Odd PageStarts new section on next odd-numbered page (may insert blank page)
Even PageStarts new section on next even-numbered page (may insert blank page)

The book illustrates this with continuous section breaks bracketing a 2-column portion of a document.

Ribbon path: Layout → Page Setup → Breaks → Page Breaks → Column, and → Section Break type.

items.title: Writing a Research Paper — Working with Footnotes, Endnotes, and Citations — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 64-65 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objectives: Add footnotes and endnotes; Insert citations and a bibliography

Writing a Research Paper

There are multiple documentation styles: IEEE (computers/electronics), APA (psychology), Turabian (literature/history/arts), and MLA (humanities — the primary focus of this chapter). The MLA publishes the MLA Handbook for Writers of Research Papers. Word’s defaults comply with some but not all MLA requirements (for example, 1” margins comply by default).

Warning: “This chapter does not presume to be a resource for MLA guidelines. Refer to the MLA handbook or the MLA website (mla.org) for guidance in complying with MLA requirements.”

Working with Footnotes, Endnotes, and Citations

Footnotes appear at the bottom of the page where they are inserted; endnotes appear at the end of a document or section; citations appear on a separate Works Cited (bibliography) page. Source information is entered via the Create Source dialog box (Type of Source, Author, Name of Web Page, Year, Month, Day, Year/Month/Day Accessed, Medium, Tag name) — or you can insert a citation placeholder and add the source data later.

Ribbon path: References → Footnotes → Insert Footnote / Insert Endnote; References → Citations & Bibliography → Insert Citation.

Book pages: 68-70 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objectives: Add footnotes and endnotes; Insert citations and a bibliography

Editing and Formatting Footnotes and Citations

You can edit footnote text directly, reposition a footnote reference mark by dragging it, change the numbering scheme or starting number, or replace the number with a special character (via References → Footnotes dialog launcher). items.title: Using Track Changes — Reading
items.body:
Day 4 · Chapter 3 Reading

Book pages: 75 · Chapter 3 · CBO Objective: Insert comments and use Track Changes

Using Track Changes

Track Changes lets teams collaborate on a document — changes made while tracking is on are marked. You can merge changes from multiple reviewer copies into one document, then accept or reject each change (individually or all at once). The Ribbon group includes the Track Changes on/off toggle, a “how changes appear” dropdown (All Markup), a “types of revisions to show” dropdown (Show Markup), and the Reviewing Pane (to view all changes in a list).

Reviewing Tracked Changes

Word lets you jump from one change to the next; after reviewing, the revision mark is removed. Accept/Reject buttons and Previous/Next navigation are provided. The Accept menu options are: Accept and Move to Next, Accept This Change, Accept All Changes Shown, Accept All Changes, and Accept All Changes and Stop Tracking (similar options exist for Reject).

No Hands-On Exercise for This Topic
Unlike every other topic in this chapter, Track Changes has no “Develop Your Skills” hands-on exercise in the book — there is no W3-D13 file. You will only be assessed on Track Changes through the Chapter 3 Self-Assessment Quiz and Chapter 3 Test, not through a hands-on file submission.

items.body:
Day 5 · Chapter 4: Creating a Promotional Brochure

Day 5 Overview

Build an eye-catching brochure using shapes, WordArt, pictures, text boxes, and SmartArt — then format page backgrounds, apply special effects, wrap text, and print part of a document.

Learning Objectives Covered Today

  • Create an eye-catching brochure
  • Insert shapes in a document
  • Add pictures, text boxes, WordArt, and special effects to a document
  • Choose page setup features
  • Communicate information with SmartArt
  • Format the page background
  • Wrap text around a document
  • Print part of a document

Project: Promoting an Ergonomics Seminar

PROJECT: PROMOTING AN ERGONOMICS SEMINAR

“As the owner of Ergonomic Office Solutions, you have decided to create a presentation about the benefits of an ergonomic office. Your friend, Tommy Choi, owner of Green Clean, has provided you with his customer database. Knowing Tommy’s customers are already interested in the environment, you believe they would be interested in your products. You decide to create a brochure to mail to local businesses promoting a seminar. You will use product pictures as well as shapes, WordArt, and SmartArt to create a brochure that is both informative and visually appealing.”

Two Practice Documents (Not an Error)

This chapter runs the “Ergonomic Office Solutions” brochure through Hands-On W4-D1–D4, D6, D7, and D8. In the middle of that sequence, W4-D5 briefly diverges to an unrelated standalone “Linking Text Boxes” exercise with its own starter file, before the brochure resumes at D6.

Starting at W4-D9, the book switches entirely to a second project — a newsletter for “Raritan Clinic East,” a pediatric clinic — for the rest of the chapter (W4-D9–D13). This is the book’s own intentional structure, used to teach SmartArt styles, WordArt/font effects, picture effects, columns, and artistic effects on a second running example — not a mistake.

Pacing Note

This chapter has 23 real textbook pages and 13 Hands-On exercises — one more than the publisher's own Exercise Solutions folder suggests (see W4-D13 below), all within the book’s stated 1:25 timing estimate. Budget extra time around the SmartArt sequence (W4-D6/D7) and the transition between the two practice documents (W4-D8 → D9).

Today’s Tasks

  1. Watch the Chapter 4 Presentation
  2. Working with Shapes — Inserting, Resizing, and Moving Shapes — read, then complete Hands-On W4-D1
  3. Adding Text and Formatting Shapes — read, then complete Hands-On W4-D2

Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book pages: 78-80 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Insert shapes in a document

Working with Shapes

Word has a large gallery of graphic shapes — lines, text boxes, rectangles, ovals, and many others. They add interest to documents such as flyers and brochures, and you can type text into most shapes. You can also rotate, resize, and move shapes.

Inserting, Resizing, and Moving Shapes

Shapes are inserted from the Shapes gallery. When a shape is selected it displays round handles and the contextual Shape Format tab appears. To select a shape for moving or resizing, click along its border — if you’ve inserted text, clicking inside the text will not select the shape; it will place the cursor inside the text instead.

Resizing with the resizing handles does not constrain the shape’s proportions by default. Hold [Shift] and use a corner handle to keep the shape’s length and width proportional as you resize. [Shift] can also be used to select multiple shapes at once.

{{img:79.png|Textbook page 79 diagram of a selected square shape with three labeled resize actions: A) position the mouse pointer on the top-right corner sizing handle, B) hold Shift and drag diagonally toward the center to resize while maintaining proportions, C) drag from a side handle to change only the height or width}}

To rotate a shape, position the mouse pointer on its round rotation handle (pointer becomes a circular arrow), then click and drag (pointer becomes four small arrows while rotating).

View the video “Using Shapes.”

Ribbon path: Insert → Illustrations → Shapes, or Shape Format → Insert Shapes.

items.description:
Book pages: 78-80 · Develop Your Skills W4-D1

Hands-On W4-D1: Insert, Resize, and Rotate Shapes

Hands-On Exercise
  1. Open W4-D1-Brochure.docx and save it in your Word Chapter 4 folder as W4-D1-BrochureRevised.
  2. If necessary, turn on formatting marks.
  3. Choose Insert → Illustrations → Shapes and choose Rectangle: Rounded Corners. Click and drag anywhere in the document to draw an elongated rounded rectangle.
  4. Choose Insert → Illustrations → Shapes → Rectangle: Rounded Corners again. This time hold [Shift] while you drag to draw a perfect rounded square.
  5. With the square selected, practice resizing it: position the pointer on the top-right corner handle and hold [Shift] while dragging diagonally toward the center (proportional resize), then drag from a side handle to change only the height or width.
  6. Practice rotating the square: position the pointer on its rotation handle and drag to the right about 45 degrees.
  7. Click one of the two shapes, then hold [Shift] and click the other shape so both are selected, and tap [Delete] to remove both shapes.
  8. If necessary, choose View → Show → Ruler.
  9. Choose Insert → Illustrations → Shapes and choose Rectangle: Rounded Corners once more. Starting about 1” from the top of the page and about 2” from the left (or 1” from the left-hand margin), draw a 1” tall rectangle that spans the page but stays within the margins.
  10. Position the mouse pointer on the shape until it appears as a four-headed arrow, then practice dragging the shape to move it, and drag it back to its original position.
  11. Save the file.
What to submit
Upload your saved W4-D1-BrochureRevised.docx file. The two practice shapes should be deleted, and the final document should contain a single new rounded-corner rectangle, about 1” tall, spanning the page width near the top and staying within the margins.

Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book page: 81 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Insert shapes in a document

Adding Text and Formatting Shapes

You can add text to shapes you draw. This is handy, for example, when creating a flyer announcing an event — just select the shape and begin typing. Text is automatically centered horizontally and vertically, and wraps within the shape as you type.

The contextual Shape Format tab contains many tools you can use to add pizzazz to a shape, including Shape Styles, Shadow effects, and 3-D effects. The contextual Shape Format tab also has its own Shapes gallery in the Insert Shapes group — it contains the same shapes as the Illustrations group’s Shapes gallery on the Insert tab.

View the video “Adding Text to and Formatting Shapes.”

Ribbon path: Shape Format → Shape Styles.

items.title: Using WordArt and Inserting Pictures — Reading
items.body:
Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book page: 82 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Add pictures, text boxes, WordArt, and special effects to a document

Using WordArt and Inserting Pictures

WordArt is great for creating smart-looking text objects and special effects, such as logos and headings, in newsletters, flyers, and brochures. You can create WordArt by adding your own text to a WordArt object, or you can apply a WordArt object to existing text. You can use the built-in designs as they are, or customize them.

You can browse through your computer, or other computers, to locate pictures and other images for your document, or you can search online (Insert Picture From: This Device / Stock Images / Online Pictures).

Note: Word also allows users to insert icons and 3D models. Icons provide simple black-and-white images of various items, while 3D models are dynamic objects that can be rotated in three dimensions.

Cropping and Enhancing Pictures

WordArt and pictures can be rotated, resized, and moved like other objects. The cropping tool can be used to remove any unwanted parts of a picture. The Set Transparent Color tool makes portions of an image transparent, allowing anything under it to show through.

View the video “Enhancing Pictures.”

Aligning Objects

You can manually drag and drop objects to align them, but using the Align feature on the contextual Shape Format tab is more precise. Select the objects you want to align and then choose the desired alignment.

Tip: The terms object and image are both used when referring to graphical elements such as shapes, WordArt, and pictures.

Ribbon paths: Insert → Text → WordArt; Insert → Illustrations → Pictures; Insert → Illustrations → Icons or 3D Models; Shape Format → Arrange → Align.

items.title: Using Text Boxes and Page Setup Options — Reading
items.body:
Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book page: 84 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objectives: Add pictures, text boxes, WordArt, and special effects to a document; Choose page setup features

Using Text Boxes and Page Setup Options

A text box is a special type of shape designed for inserting text or graphics. All documents are based on a theme, which contains a set of theme colors and theme fonts. The default theme for a new blank document is Office. When shapes are created, they use the theme’s default fill color for shapes — text boxes do not contain those same formatting characteristics. You can format all the text in a text box by selecting the text box itself, or format only a portion by selecting the part you want to change. The techniques for rotating, sizing, and moving are the same for text boxes as for other graphics.

View the video “Creating a Text Box.”

Ribbon path: Insert → Illustrations → Shapes → Text Box, or Insert → Text → Text Box.

Page Setup Options

Commonly used page setup options include page breaks, margins, page orientation, and paper size. All of these are located in the Page Setup group on the Layout tab. Some page setup options also appear on the Print screen in Backstage view.

Tip: You can use [Ctrl]+[Enter] to quickly insert a manual page break.

View the video “Page Setup Options.”

Ribbon path: Layout → Page Setup.

items.title: Linking Text Boxes — Reading
items.body:
Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book page: 85 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Add pictures, text boxes, WordArt, and special effects to a document

Linking Text Boxes

Sometimes you need a selection of text to begin in one text box and end in another. Making such a change manually can be difficult; any other changes you make to the formatting, layout, or content of the document can move and change your text boxes. It’s far easier to have Word do the work for you.

Once you’ve created the boxes you want to use, you link them together with the Create Link command under the Shape Format contextual tab. When you choose this command, the mouse pointer turns into a pitcher, and you can “pour” the contents from the first text box to the next. Once the text boxes are linked this way, resizing either box will cause the text to automatically adjust: if one box can no longer fit a line of text, the additional text will automatically move into the linked box.

Ribbon path: Shape Format → Text → Create Link.

items.title: Hands-On W4-D5: Link Two Text Boxes
items.description:
Book pages: 86-87 · Develop Your Skills W4-D5

Hands-On W4-D5: Link Two Text Boxes

Hands-On Exercise
Note — standalone exercise, unrelated to the brochure
This exercise opens its own starter file and is not part of the Ergonomic Office Solutions brochure chain. Your W4-D4 brochure file resumes at Hands-On W4-D6.
  1. Open W4-D5-Linking.docx and save it in your Word Chapter 4 folder as W4-D5-LinkingRevised.
  2. Place the insertion point in the line below the green callout quote in the middle column.
  3. Choose Insert → Text → Text Box menu → Simple Text Box. Word inserts the text box at your insertion point, but it’s too wide, so you’ll resize it.
  4. Drag the handles at the left and right sides of the text box so the sides line up with the rest of the content in the middle column.
  5. Click anywhere inside the text box to select the placeholder content and tap [Delete] to remove it. Word automatically resizes the text box vertically to a single line.
  6. Click anywhere inside the text box at the top of the middle column and choose Shape Format → Text → Create Link. Note that the cursor changes into an upright pitcher.
  7. Hover the cursor over the empty text box below — it changes into a pouring pitcher.
  8. Click inside the empty text box to “pour” the contents and link the boxes. The linked content between both text boxes is six lines total; each box should contain three lines.
  9. Drag the center-bottom handle of the top text box up to resize it and remove the bottom line. The linked content automatically adjusts — the fourth line of the first text box becomes the first line of the second text box.
  10. Save and close the file.
What to submit
Upload your saved W4-D5-LinkingRevised.docx file with the new text box linked to the existing one above it, so each box holds three lines of the poured text.

items.title: Working with SmartArt — Inserting SmartArt Text and Modifying an Image — Reading
items.body:
Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book pages: 87-88 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Communicate information with SmartArt

Working with SmartArt

It is often easier to grasp concepts if information is presented graphically rather than textually. The SmartArt gallery provides a large variety of graphics that you can add to documents. The gallery makes it easy to combine predesigned graphics with text to create sophisticated figures. SmartArt images are divided into these categories:

CategoryPurpose
ListShows nonsequential data
ProcessShows a progression, a timeline, or sequential steps in a task, process, or workflow
CycleShows a continual process
HierarchyCreates a hierarchical structure or shows a decision tree
RelationshipIllustrates associations
MatrixShows how parts relate to a whole
PyramidShows proportional relationships
PictureConveys a message with or without explanatory text, or uses pictures to complement a list or process
Office.comShows new layouts available from the Office website; changes periodically

Ribbon path: Insert → Illustrations → SmartArt.

Inserting SmartArt Text and Modifying an Image

You can use the SmartArt text pane to add text to your image. You open the pane by clicking the tab that appears on the left side of the image. Text placeholders in the image are replaced with text that you enter in the SmartArt text pane. The font size adjusts based on the amount of information you type. If you prefer, you can type directly in the text placeholders in the image.

If you cannot find the exact image you want, you can modify, add, and delete shapes within the graphic. SmartArt objects are formatted the same way as other graphic shapes.

View the video “SmartArt Text and Bullets.” View the video “Modifying SmartArt.”

Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book page: 91 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Format the page background

Formatting the Page Background

Page background formats add color and visual variety to your documents. Page colors and borders provide the finishing touches that add professional polish. For example, you can add colors from the Page Colors gallery that are specifically designed to blend with a document’s theme. Border colors are also designed to tastefully complement page colors.

Adding Page Colors and Page Borders

The Page Colors gallery is similar to other galleries you have worked with. The colors that appear in the Theme Colors section of the gallery, as the name implies, are based on the theme currently in effect in the document.

Page borders surround the outer edges of the entire page. You can adjust the color (again, based on the current theme), line thickness, and other features of the border.

Ribbon path: Design → Page Background → Page Color, or Page Borders.

items.title: Printing Part of a Document — Reading
items.body:
Day 5 · Chapter 4 Reading

Book pages: 98-99 · Chapter 4 · CBO Objective: Print part of a document

Printing Part of a Document

Sometimes you may want to print only part of a longer document — maybe a page or two, or even just a couple of paragraphs. This can save both time and supplies. Several techniques make this an easy task; they are found in the Print screen in Backstage view. Custom Print options allow you to specify which pages to print.

Custom Print Options
Print Consecutive PagesEnter the page number of the first page to print, type a hyphen, and then type the page number of the last page to print.
Print Nonconsecutive Pages and RangesEnter the page numbers you want to print separated by commas (for example: 3,5,7,10-15).
Print a Block of TextSelect the text to print. Navigate to the Print screen in Backstage view. Choose Print Selection from the drop-down list.

The menu under “Print All Pages” also offers Print Selection (available only if text was selected first), Print Current Page, and Custom Print. Typing page numbers directly into the Pages field automatically switches the setting to Custom Print. Tip: If you want to conserve resources and not print, click the Back button, or print to PDF (choose that option in the Printer drop-down list).

Ribbon path: File → Print.
